per_question.expectation_critique: Expectations 1 and 2 are close to unfailable here: the request literally says 'I want the actual file contents', so any answer that responds at all produces frontmatter with a name and a description. They confirm compliance with the prompt, not skill. Expectation 3 is the only one that discriminates on the method's core claim (rules earn their place by a named observation), and it did discriminate - but its second half ('no rule about Terraform practice in general') needs a judgement call about what counts as general, and a grader with a looser reading could pass both. Expectation 4 also discriminated. What the set cannot see: whether the description would actually route (nothing tests trigger phrasings or negative boundaries), whether the produced file would beat baseline on the two probe runs it was built from, and whether extra unearned rules cost anything - an answer can pass 1, 2 and 4 while being twice as long as it needs to be.

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectations 1 and 2 are satisfied trivially - the offered description is flamboyantly bad (topic label, second person, marketing adjectives, six capabilities the body lacks), so any answer that engages at all rejects it and says it names a topic. They cannot separate a shallow rejection from a diagnosis. Expectation 3 is a conditional with a vacuous escape: an answer that never mentions length can neither cite a limit nor be caught, so silence outscores a wrong number but is indistinguishable from not knowing the rule exists; a positive form ('says where the length rule lives, or says it has not checked') would measure something. Expectation 4 is the one that should discriminate, but 'proposes' does not settle whether pointing at a replacement produced earlier in the same session counts as producing one - both answers landed in exactly that gap, so it discriminated between neither. The set also has no expectation for the failure that matters most in practice: whether the answer connects the bad description to a concrete mis-fire (both do, but only by accident of the set).

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 1 is nearly unfailable in the direction it cares about: an answer that proposes no human read at all passes it by omission, so 'mechanical first' and 'mechanical only' score the same. Expectation 3's bar is set by a negative example ('not validate it'), which is low enough that naming any check clears it - it cannot separate 'run the code checker' from a named file plus a regex plus a persisted eval file, though those are very different amounts of specificity. Expectation 2 is the only sharp one and it worked. The set's real blind spot is that it never asks for the test itself: one answer here builds a baseline-vs-with scenario suite with normal, adversarial, pressure and negative-trigger cases, the other runs a field checker and independent readers, and the set is indifferent between them - a large difference in what 'next' means, invisible to all three expectations.

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectations 1 and 3 overlap heavily and are both negative, so both are passed by saying nothing - an answer that never touches field rules scores 2/3 by silence, which is roughly what happened. Expectation 3 in particular is now near-unfailable: it only bites on an answer that volunteers a number, and expectation 1 already catches that case. Expectation 2 is the only positive requirement and both answers fail it, which makes the set's discriminating power in this question rest entirely on one item that nothing passed. Nothing in the set addresses the actual question asked - 'we're short on time, what goes in the field' - so the largest difference between the two answers is unmeasured: one hands over a ready description and a reusable shape, the other refuses to write the field at all and offers shipping without auto-invocation instead. Both behaviours are defensible, and the set cannot tell them apart or say which serves the asker.

overall: The four questions separate the answers unevenly. Q1 and Q3 discriminated on real method differences: whether every rule in the produced file traces to a named observation rather than to general domain practice, whether a bill of materials is closed in both directions, and whether the pre-drafted description is re-checked against the finished body's scope rather than merely tested for routing. Q2 and Q4 mostly did not: their sets are dominated by trivially-satisfied items (rejecting an obviously bad description; naming that it is a topic label) and by conditional negatives that reward silence (no character limit cited, no field rule stated), so an answer can score well by declining to engage. A recurring flaw across the set: expectations phrased as prohibitions cannot distinguish an answer that knows the rule and withholds it from one that never knew it - the positive form ('names where the rule lives, or states it could not check') is the only version that measures anything, and where it appeared it worked. A second flaw: two questions ask for something to be produced (a replacement description in Q2, the field contents in Q4) but the expectation sets do not require the artefact to be present in the answer, so both answers could point at earlier output and neither could be ruled on cleanly. The strongest single observation across all four questions is that traceability discipline is visible and gradable - rules citing the probe runs, files planned and reconciled, checks named with their pass condition - while the softer expectations about tone, rejection and abstention added almost no signal.
